title: Drill: heap-sort descending
prompt: From memory: return `nums` sorted DESCENDING by pushing everything into a max-heap and polling into the result. (Drills the comparator flip + drain loop.)

solution.explanation: A reversed comparator turns Java's min-heap into a max-heap, so each poll returns the largest remaining value. n offers and n polls give O(n log n) time and O(n) space. `Integer.compare` avoids the overflow that `b - a` risks.

hints: A min-heap always hands back the smallest element. What change makes it hand back the largest?
Give the `PriorityQueue` a reversed comparator: `(a, b) -> Integer.compare(b, a)`.
Offer every value, then fill `res[i] = maxHeap.poll();` for i from 0 to n - 1.

title: Template: size-k heap
explanation: Offer everything, and evict the smallest once the heap holds more than k values. What remains is the k largest, and their minimum, `peek()`, is the k-th largest. The check is `> k`, not `>= k`: the heap should settle at exactly k values.

title: Drill: k largest (size-k min-heap)
prompt: From memory (size-k min-heap): return the `k` largest values of `nums` in any order. Offer everything, evict the smallest whenever the heap exceeds k, then drain it.

solution.explanation: The min-heap's top is always the weakest of the values kept, so evicting it whenever the size goes over k keeps exactly the k largest seen so far. O(n log k) time, O(k) space.

hints: If the heap may hold only k values, which value should be easiest to throw out when a new one arrives?
Use a min-heap (the default `PriorityQueue`): offer each number, and `poll()` whenever `size() > k`.
After the loop the heap holds exactly the k largest. Drain it: `res[i] = heap.poll();`.

title: Which heap?
prompt: "Return the k points closest to the origin." To keep memory at O(k), you maintain…
options: A MAX-heap of size k ordered by distance — evict the farthest whenever size exceeds k
A min-heap of size k — evict the closest
A max-heap of all n points
explanation: Mirror image of k-th largest: to KEEP the smallest k, the heap's top must be the current worst (largest distance) so it can be evicted. Keep-smallest → max-heap; keep-largest → min-heap.

title: Two heaps: which is which?
prompt: In the two-heap running median, why is the **lower** half stored in a **max**-heap?
options: Its top must be the largest value of the lower half, the one right next to the median
So `findMedian` can poll every element in order
Because the stream may contain negative numbers
explanation: The median depends only on the values at the boundary between the halves: the largest of the lower half and the smallest of the upper half. A max-heap puts the first at its top and a min-heap puts the second at its top, so both are O(1) to peek.

title: Template: two-heap median
prompt: Complete `addNum` and `findMedian`. `small` holds the lower half and may have one more element than `large`.
explanation: Moving `small`'s maximum into `large` keeps every lower-half value ≤ every upper-half value. Moving one back when `large` gets bigger keeps the sizes equal or `small` one larger. With an odd count, the median is `small.peek()`.

title: Drill: merge k sorted arrays
prompt: From memory (k-way merge with a heap): each `lists[i]` is sorted ascending. Return one ascending array with every element. Keep at most one entry per list in the heap.
hints: The smallest remaining element is always at the front of one of the lists. How can you find the smallest of k fronts quickly, again and again?
Use a min-heap of `int[]{value, listIndex, elementIndex}`, seeded with index 0 of every non-empty list.
Poll the smallest entry, write its value, then `if (next < lists[li].length) heap.offer(new int[]{lists[li][next], li, next});`.

solution.explanation: The heap holds only the current front of each list, so its top is always the smallest element not yet output. After polling it, that list's next element takes its place. N total elements with a heap of size at most k give O(N log k) time and O(k) extra space (plus the output array).
